rationale: Trivially repeatable token forgery yields unrestricted flight authorisation for rogue operators across the volume.
Unauthenticated civil GNSS is a publicly known single point of failure whose spoofing or jamming directly causes loss of control or restricted-airspace incursion.
Automated tooling finds and repeats injection easily, giving mass record exfiltration and corruption but only indirect flight-safety effects.
Requires compromising or impersonating a third-party provider, but falsified meteorological or traffic data drives genuinely unsafe routing decisions region-wide.
Weak identity proofing is easy to probe and abuse, though impact is mainly accountability loss and unattributable flights rather than immediate hazard.
Cheap RF jamming and unencrypted MAVLink are well documented, and C2 loss during BVLOS leads directly to fail-safe descent or crash.
Needs prior privileged access and causes no direct airspace hazard, but destroys the forensic record needed to detect and correct other attacks.
Insider-level access to regulator systems is hard to obtain, yet undetected USSP non-compliance erodes oversight across the whole federation.
Firmware backdooring demands hardware access and skill but hands an adversary full authority over the airframe, with catastrophic consequences.
Unvalidated telemetry ingest lets injected tracks mask genuine conflicts, degrading the shared traffic picture for every participant in the volume.
A trusted-vendor or component compromise is extremely difficult to mount and to discover, but a single success backdoors the entire deployed fleet.
Poisoning the single source of truth propagates corrupted state simultaneously to every dependent U-Space service with no independent cross-check.
Physical sabotage needs on-site presence and affects one facility, but a compromised vertiport endangers aircraft and people on the ground during landing.
Absent sensor-fusion validation allows injected altitude or IMU data to drive erroneous flight decisions and loss-of-control events.
Ground-station power loss halts operations and BMS manipulation can deplete a battery in flight, though both need targeted access.
Leaked keys are easy to find and reuse at scale for bulk flight-plan exfiltration, but the harm is confidentiality and reconnaissance rather than safety.
Deleting or altering a no-fly boundary silently authorises incursions into protected airspace such as airport approaches.
Insider exfiltration of strategic plans is hard to execute and has no immediate operational effect, though it informs later targeted attacks.
Flooding a single unprotected gateway is cheap and endlessly repeatable, denying authorisation services to every user in the volume until mitigated.
Unauthenticated geofence feeds let injected boundaries steer many compliant aircraft into controlled or restricted airspace.
Published legislative ambiguity is visible to anyone and exploitable without technical attack, weakening sector-wide security posture over time.
